result: Population imaging reveals functional segregation of Purkinje cell activity across the cerebellum. Three spatially-clustered regions were identified along the rostrocaudal axis, with responses to whole-field flashes enriched in a bilaterally symmetric central region, responses to rotational motion asymmetrically localized in the caudolateral cerebellum, and motor responses broadly distributed. Sensory responses to visual features are more anatomically clustered than motor responses.
evaluation: Claims C2, C30-C33, C38-C40 collectively demonstrate spatial organization of Purkinje cell activity using multilinear regression analysis of calcium imaging data (N=10 fish). The functional segregation is supported by quantitative analysis showing distinct spatial patterns for different visual and motor features, with principal component analysis confirming four spatially-clustered functional regions.

result: Electrophysiological recordings reveal that Purkinje cells can be assigned to three visual complex spike phenotypes. Complex spikes were evoked by a narrow subset of stimuli (mean 6.0±0.4 nonzero coefficients out of 22), with 60/61 cells assignable to one of three visual phenotypes: directionally-selective translational motion onset (N=31/61), directionally-selective rotational velocity (N=14/61), or changes in luminance (N=25/61). These phenotypes showed spatial organization with rostromedial clustering for motion onset responses and caudolateral clustering for rotational velocity responses.
evaluation: Claims C3, C49-C64 are strongly supported by comprehensive electrophysiological recordings from 61 Purkinje cells with multilinear regression analysis using elastic net optimization. The classification into three visual phenotypes is quantitatively demonstrated with clear spatial mapping onto a reference cerebellum. Statistical rigor is appropriate with N=61 cells from 61 fish.

result: Simple spike output of most Purkinje cells is strongly driven by motor-related signals. Motor activity significantly modulated simple spike activity in nearly all Purkinje cells (N=60/61) and was the main contributor in the majority (N=44/61). Mean simple spike firing rates were twice as high during swim bouts compared to rest (14.5±1.5 Hz vs 7.6±0.8 Hz, p<0.001). Simple spike responses were broader than complex spike responses, with swim vigor being the strongest motor contributor.
evaluation: Claims C4, C100-C108 are well-supported by multilinear regression analysis of electrophysiological data from 61 cells. The statistical significance is properly demonstrated (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test), and the finding that motor activity dominates simple spike responses is quantitatively robust across the population.

result: The largest group of Purkinje cells (N=33/61) showed direction-selective responses to translational motion onset. These responses typically spanned two of four cardinal directions, producing on average one complex spike at motion onset (1.2±0.6 spikes/stimulus). Direction selectivity index ranged from 0.2 to 0.9. Complex spike occurrence was independent of behavioral response, with reverse visual motion (which evokes no swimming) equally well-represented as directions that drive swimming. Cells showed hemispheric lateralization in directional preference.
evaluation: Claims C65-C72 are supported by detailed electrophysiological analysis with quantitative metrics. The independence of complex spikes from behavioral response (C67-C68) is a critical finding that distinguishes sensory from motor encoding. The directional tuning analysis and hemispheric lateralization patterns are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes.

result: The second group of Purkinje cells (N=12/61) in the caudolateral cerebellum showed sustained, directionally-selective increases in complex spikes during rotational motion. Complex spike firing rates were 2-5 times higher than baseline during preferred direction motion (mean increase=340±40%), while rates during non-preferred direction fell below baseline (0.32±0.1 Hz vs 0.87±0.1 Hz baseline). Responses were highly lateralized: all clockwise-preferring cells (10/10) were in the left hemisphere, while counter-clockwise-preferring cells (2/2) were in the right hemisphere. Spontaneous complex spike rates were strongly depressed following robust responses (37±16% of baseline).
evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are strongly supported by quantitative electrophysiological data with clear statistical measures. The complete lateralization (10/10 and 2/2) is striking and well-documented. The homeostatic regulation finding (C79) is novel and quantitatively characterized. Sample sizes are adequate for the claims made.

result: The third group of Purkinje cells (N=25/61) had complex spike responses correlated with luminance changes that were heterogeneous in feature encoding. Cells encoded either luminance increases (9/25), decreases (11/25), or both (5/25), with locations mixed across the central cerebellum. Most responses were transient (mean=0.80±0.02 spikes per luminance change). Two cells showed sustained rate coding of ambient luminance that did not adapt over tens of minutes (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni correction).
evaluation: Claims C80-C85 are supported by electrophysiological data with appropriate statistical testing. The heterogeneity of this group is well-characterized quantitatively. The sustained ambient luminance encoding in two cells (C85) is properly tested statistically and represents an interesting subpopulation, though the small N=2 limits generalizability.

result: Different Purkinje cell groups showed distinct baseline complex spike firing rates. Rotational motion velocity-responsive cells had significantly higher baseline rates than motion onset-responsive cells (0.77±0.1 Hz vs 0.20±0.02 Hz, p<0.001, Bonferroni correction). Luminance and motor-responsive cells had intermediate rates (0.28±0.1 Hz and 0.34±0.1 Hz respectively).
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by quantitative comparison across groups with appropriate statistical testing (one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc correction). The significant difference between groups provides additional functional characterization of the three regions.

result: Zebrafish Purkinje cells can be divided into two anatomical populations based on axonal projections: internally-projecting (contacting eurydendroid cells) and externally-projecting caudal axons (contacting vestibular nuclei). Strikingly, 6/7 Purkinje cells with caudal axons exhibited rotational motion complex spike phenotype, whereas only 1/10 cells with internal axons had this phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by combined electrophysiology and anatomical reconstruction (N=17 cells from 17 fish). The strong association between axonal projection pattern and complex spike phenotype (6/7 vs 1/10) is statistically compelling despite modest sample size. C88 is also supported by prior literature citations.

result: Motor regressors did not significantly contribute to complex spike activity in the majority of Purkinje cells (N=49/61). Some complex spikes correlated with swimming even without visual stimuli, but these responses were unreliable (mean probability=0.38±0.07 for stimulus trials, N=9 cells) with variable latencies from bout onset. Motor-responsive cells were distributed across the cerebellum without apparent clustering.
evaluation: Claims C92-C97 are supported by multilinear regression analysis and analysis of blank trials. The unreliability and variable latencies of motor-related complex spikes (C94-C95) contrast with the stereotyped visual responses, supporting the conclusion that complex spikes primarily encode sensory information. The lack of spatial clustering (C97) further distinguishes motor from visual complex spike responses.

result: Complex spike responses during rotational visual motion are predominantly sensory rather than motor. In semi-paralyzed fish with eye tracking, the majority of caudolateral Purkinje cells showed stereotyped complex spike responses to directional rotational stimuli that did not correlate well with variable eye movements across trials.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by additional experiments in semi-paralyzed fish (N=11) with simultaneous eye tracking and electrophysiology. The multilinear regression analysis with 12 eye motor regressors showed that only 2/13 cells had motor-dominant complex spikes, and further analysis revealed these were better explained by sensory features. This is a critical control experiment.

result: Calcium signals in Purkinje cells report both complex spikes and simple spike bursts. Every complex spike elicited a dendritic calcium peak, but isolated simple spike bursts also produced widespread dendritic calcium increases of smaller amplitude but similar duration. The majority of calcium signal is driven by complex spikes (mean=78.4±6.8%, N=8 cells), though simple spikes can account for up to half the signal in some cells. Somatic and dendritic signals were highly correlated (mean=0.87±0.2, N=5 cells).
evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are well-supported by simultaneous electrophysiology and calcium imaging experiments (N=8 cells from 8 fish). The multilinear regression analysis quantifying relative contributions is appropriate. This is an important methodological finding that affects interpretation of all calcium imaging data. The high soma-dendrite correlation (C46) suggests limited spatial segregation of inputs in zebrafish Purkinje cells.

result: Granule cell activity was strong and widespread during swimming in both somatic and parallel fiber layers, with weaker but widespread activity during eye movements. Electrophysiological recordings revealed several granule cells (N=6/8) with negligible baseline firing but large increases during fictive bouts (1.3±0.3 Hz at rest vs 25.7±7.6 Hz during bouts, p<0.005). Half of motor-excited granule cells (N=3/6) showed significant spike autocorrelations during swimming (p<0.001) at frequencies comparable to fictive swim frequency (mean difference=1.3±0.6 Hz). These findings suggest motor efference copies are relayed to many granule cells, which drive broad motor-related activation of Purkinje cell simple spikes.
evaluation: Claims C116-C124 are supported by both population imaging (N=7 fish) and single-cell electrophysiology (N=8 cells from 8 fish). The autocorrelation analysis (C121-C122) provides strong evidence for motor efference signals with appropriate statistical testing (Ljung-Box Q-test). The integration of imaging and electrophysiology data strengthens the conclusions about motor efference pathways.

result: Simple spikes in zebrafish Purkinje cells do not show significant autocorrelations at any frequency during spontaneous fictive bouts, unlike the highly autocorrelated ventral root signal (mean frequency=26.7±0.7 Hz, N=30 fish). Simple spikes are not modulated in phase with rhythmic swimming but are graded by swim strength, suggesting individual Purkinje cells do not encode activation of individual muscles.
evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by autocorrelation analysis of electrophysiological data. The contrast between rhythmic ventral root activity and non-rhythmic simple spike activity is clear and well-documented. The inference that Purkinje cells do not encode individual muscle activation (C112) is reasonable given the lack of phase-locking, though this is an indirect conclusion.

result: Interactions between complex and simple spikes show heterogeneous modulation patterns across Purkinje cells that become temporally restricted during swimming. The acute effect of a complex spike on simple spike rates was identical between motor and non-motor periods for only 50 milliseconds following the complex spike, after which simple spiking returned to high levels during ongoing behavior. This temporal window was consistent across cells regardless of whether baseline modulation was pause or facilitation. The behavioral state temporally restricts complex spike effects on simple spike output, with implications for plasticity mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C132-C139 are supported by detailed temporal analysis of complex spike-simple spike relationships under different behavioral contexts. The 50 ms temporal window finding (C136-C137) is novel and quantitatively characterized. The statistical analysis comparing motor vs non-motor contexts is appropriate (Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.05). The inference about plasticity implications (C138-C139) is reasonable but speculative.

result: Purkinje cells preferentially encode visual features in complex spike activity while swimming activity is predominantly encoded by simple spikes. Purkinje cells with visual complex spike phenotypes have simple spike activity correlated most strongly with motor activity (fraction from motor regressors=0.65±0.05, 0.54±0.07, 0.76±0.02 for the three phenotypes). In contrast, cells with motor-related complex spike phenotypes have lower motor contribution to simple spikes (0.35±0.12) and broader sensory-motor integration. This suggests sensory and motor information is preferentially combined from distinct sources.
evaluation: Claims C126-C129 are supported by comprehensive multilinear regression analysis across all 61 cells. The quantitative characterization of how different complex spike phenotypes relate to simple spike responses is novel and well-documented. This represents an important synthesis of the major findings about information flow in cerebellar circuits.

result: The number of Purkinje cells in larval zebrafish at seven dpf is 433±19 (mean±std, N=3), estimated using 3D template matching of nuclear-localized GCaMP6s. This is higher than the previously reported range of 180-360 Purkinje cells.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by quantitative analysis using 3D template matching on confocal stacks (N=3 fish). The methodology is appropriate for counting nuclear-localized fluorescent markers. The discrepancy with prior literature (C29) is noted but not explained; this could reflect methodological differences or developmental variation.

result: Visual stimuli elicit graded, episodic swim bouts and eye movements that vary across trials. Whole-field gratings elicited reflexive but variable optomotor responses in a probabilistic manner modulated by direction and speed. Windmill patterns elicited optokinetic eye responses with behavioral variability. Moderate intensity flashes evoked no acute behavioral response. Swimming activity is only moderately correlated with forward visual motion on a trial-by-trial basis (mean correlation=0.31±0.2).
evaluation: Claims C23-C27, C48 are supported by behavioral tracking data during experiments. The moderate correlation between swimming and visual motion (C48) is critical for the multilinear regression approach, as it allows disambiguation of sensory and motor responses. The behavioral characterization is thorough and appropriate for the experimental design.

result: Purkinje cell dendrites generally had a classic albeit simplified morphology with mostly planar dendrites oriented orthogonally to the axis of parallel fiber extension, as seen in mammalian cerebellum.
evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by morphological analysis with quantitative assessment of dendritic planarity using principal component analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The comparison to mammalian cerebellum is supported by citations. This is a useful anatomical characterization but not a primary finding.

result: Background claims about cerebellar anatomy, physiology, and function in vertebrates including zebrafish. These include established principles about Purkinje cell inputs (climbing fibers and parallel fibers), spike types (complex and simple spikes), cerebellar organization, and functional roles.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C22, C130-C131 are background knowledge claims supported by extensive literature citations. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and comprehensive.

result: Background claims about motor efference pathways to granule cells. A disynaptic pathway from spinal premotor interneurons to granule cells via lateral reticular nucleus conveys spinal cord activity. Growing evidence shows granule cells are strongly driven by locomotor activity across species. In electric fish, >90% of granule cells receive motor efference signals, though only ~20% spike.
evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are background knowledge supported by literature citations. These provide important context for interpreting the granule cell findings but are not novel results from this study.

result: Complex spikes do not show phase-locking with stereotyped locomotor movements, consistent with prior observations.
evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by a citation to previous literature (Apps, 1999) and is consistent with the variable latencies observed in this study (C95). This is confirmatory rather than novel.
